preamble.summary: A collection of miscellaneous proverbs covering a wide range of ethical topics: avoid evil and it will avoid you; do not seek public office or judicial authority presumptuously; do not neglect prayer or almsgiving; do not mock or deceive; honor the priesthood and give the prescribed offerings; care for the sick and the dead; rejoice with the joyful and mourn with the mourning; treat daughters and wives wisely; honor slaves who serve faithfully.
preamble.remarkable: The section on honoring the priesthood (vv. 29-33) is one of the most explicit endorsements of the Levitical system in the wisdom literature. The instruction to visit the sick, attend funerals, and remember death (vv. 33-40) became central to the Christian corporal works of mercy. The closing reflection on death ('Remember your last things') was foundational for the medieval ars moriendi tradition.
preamble.friction: The advice on daughters (vv. 24-25) reflects patriarchal anxieties about female sexuality and the economic burden of dowry. The instruction to 'give her to a sensible man' treats the daughter as property to be disposed of. These verses require honest acknowledgment of their cultural context.
preamble.connections: Leviticus 7:28-36 (priestly portions); Deuteronomy 18:1-5 (Levitical rights); Romans 12:15 (rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep); Matthew 25:36 (I was sick and you visited me); Ecclesiastes 7:2 (better to go to a house of mourning).

verses.text_latin: Noli facere mala et non te adprehendent.
verses.rendering: Do no evil, and evil will not overtake you.
translator_notes: A terse statement of the retribution principle: the deed shapes the consequence.

verses.text_latin: Discede ab iniquo et deficient mala abs te.
verses.rendering: Depart from injustice, and evils will depart from you.

verses.text_latin: Fili non semines mala in sulcis iniustitiae et non metes ea in septuplum.
verses.rendering: My son, do not sow evils in the furrows of injustice, and you will not reap them sevenfold.
translator_notes: The agricultural metaphor: sin sown yields a harvest multiplied sevenfold -- the symbolic number of completeness.

verses.text_latin: Noli quaerere ab homine ducatum neque a rege cathedram honoris.
verses.rendering: Do not seek from anyone a position of leadership, nor from the king a seat of honor.
translator_notes: Ambition for public office is not condemned outright but the seeking of it is warned against; authority should be received, not grasped.

key_terms.note: The cathedra is a chair of authority; the phrase evokes both judicial and academic power.

verses.text_latin: Non te iustifices ante Deum quoniam agnitor cordis ipse est et penes regem noli velle videri sapiens.
verses.rendering: Do not justify yourself before God, for he is the knower of hearts; and before the king do not seek to appear wise.
translator_notes: Self-justification before God is futile because he sees the heart; self-promotion before the king is dangerous because it invites scrutiny.

key_terms.note: A title for God that emphasizes his omniscient penetration of human motives.

verses.text_latin: Noli quaerere fieri iudex nisi valeas virtute inrumpere iniquitates ne forte extimescas faciem potentis et ponas scandalum in aequitate tua.
verses.rendering: Do not seek to become a judge unless you have the strength to break through injustice, lest you fear the face of the powerful and place a stumbling block in your own integrity.
translator_notes: Judicial office requires the courage to resist the powerful; without it, the judge becomes complicit in injustice.

verses.text_latin: Non pecces in multitudinem civitatis nec te inmittas in populum.
verses.rendering: Do not sin against the multitude of the city, and do not cast yourself into the crowd.
translator_notes: Warning against both offending the public and losing oneself in mob behavior.

verses.text_latin: Neque alliges bis peccatum in uno enim non eris inmunis.
verses.rendering: Do not bind sin to sin, for even in one you will not go unpunished.

verses.text_latin: Noli esse pusillanimis in animo tuo.
verses.rendering: Do not be faint-hearted in your spirit.

key_terms.note: Literally 'small-souled'; the opposite of magnanimous. A person without the courage to act on conviction.

verses.text_latin: Non despicias orare et facere eleemosynam.
verses.rendering: Do not neglect to pray and to give alms.
translator_notes: Prayer and almsgiving are paired as the two essential spiritual practices -- a pairing that persists into Christianity and Islam.

verses.text_latin: Ne dicas in respectu Dei miserebitur et in multitudine munerum meorum respiciet.
verses.rendering: Do not say, 'God will look upon my many offerings and accept them.'
translator_notes: Quantity of offerings does not guarantee divine favor; the quality of the heart matters more.

verses.text_latin: Non inrideas hominem in amaritudine animae suae est enim qui humiliat et exaltat circumspector Deus.
verses.rendering: Do not mock a person in the bitterness of his soul, for there is one who humbles and exalts -- God who sees all.
translator_notes: Mocking another's suffering invites divine reversal: the mocker may be humbled, the mocked exalted.

key_terms.note: God as the all-seeing observer who misses nothing; every act of cruelty is witnessed.

verses.text_latin: Noli arare mendacium adversus fratrem tuum neque in amicum similiter facias.
verses.rendering: Do not plow a lie against your brother, and do not do the same to your friend.
translator_notes: 'Plowing a lie' extends the agricultural imagery: falsehood is a crop deliberately cultivated.

verses.text_latin: Noli velle mentiri omne mendacium adsiduitas enim illius non est bona.
verses.rendering: Do not choose to tell any lie, for the habit of lying brings no good.

verses.text_latin: Noli verbosus esse in multitudine presbyterorum et non iteres verbum in oratione tua.
verses.rendering: Do not be wordy in the assembly of elders, and do not repeat yourself in your prayer.
translator_notes: Brevity in both public speech and prayer is commended; cf. Jesus' warning against vain repetitions (Matthew 6:7).

verses.text_latin: Non oderis laboriosa opera et rusticationem creatam ab Altissimo.
verses.rendering: Do not hate laborious work, nor farming, which was created by the Most High.
translator_notes: Agricultural labor is dignified as God's own creation; contempt for manual work is a form of ingratitude.

key_terms.note: Rusticatio encompasses all rural labor; Ben Sira, writing in an urban context, defends the dignity of agrarian life.

verses.text_latin: Non te reputes in multitudine indisciplinatorum.
verses.rendering: Do not count yourself among the multitude of the undisciplined.

verses.text_latin: Memento irae quoniam non tardabit.
verses.rendering: Remember wrath, for it will not delay.
translator_notes: A terse memento: divine judgment is not distant.

verses.text_latin: Humilia valde spiritum tuum quoniam vindicta carnis impii ignis et vermis.
verses.rendering: Humble your spirit deeply, for the punishment of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms.
translator_notes: Fire and worms as images of judgment derive from Isaiah 66:24 and influenced later depictions of Gehenna.

key_terms.note: The dual punishment imagery: fire consumes and worms devour. Both signify complete destruction of the impenitent.

verses.text_latin: Noli praevaricari in amicum pecuniam differentem nec fratrem carissimum auro spreveris.
verses.rendering: Do not betray a friend who defers payment, and do not despise your dearest brother for the sake of gold.
translator_notes: Friendship and kinship outweigh financial claims; to sacrifice relationship for money is a form of betrayal.

verses.text_latin: Noli discedere a muliere sensata et bona quam sortitus es in timore Domini gratia enim verecundiae illius super aurum.
verses.rendering: Do not abandon a sensible and good wife whom you have received in the fear of the Lord, for the grace of her modesty is worth more than gold.
translator_notes: The good wife is a divine gift received 'in the fear of the Lord'; her moral beauty exceeds material wealth.

key_terms.note: Verecundia means a sense of shame, propriety, and restraint; in a wife it represents moral composure.

verses.text_latin: Non laedas servum in veritate operantem neque mercennarium dantem animam suam.
verses.rendering: Do not mistreat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired laborer who devotes his life to you.
translator_notes: Protection of laborers -- both slave and free -- is a matter of justice, not mere kindness.

key_terms.note: The mercennarius works for wages; his vulnerability to exploitation is a recurring concern in Torah and prophetic literature.

verses.text_latin: Servum sensatum diligat anima tua non defraudes illum libertate neque egenum derelinquas illum.
verses.rendering: Let your soul love a wise servant; do not defraud him of his freedom, and do not abandon him to destitution.
translator_notes: The instruction to love a wise servant and not withhold freedom reflects the Israelite tradition of manumission (Deuteronomy 15:12-18).

verses.text_latin: Pecora tibi sunt adtende illis et si sunt utilia perseverent apud te.
verses.rendering: If you have cattle, attend to them; and if they are profitable, keep them.
translator_notes: Practical wisdom about livestock management, but the principle extends to all stewardship of resources.

verses.text_latin: Filii tibi sunt erudi illos et curva illos a pueritia illorum.
verses.rendering: If you have sons, instruct them, and bend them to discipline from their youth.
translator_notes: 'Curva' (bend) suggests shaping character while it is still pliable; early formation is decisive.

verses.text_latin: Filiae tibi sunt serva corpus illarum et non ostendas hilarem faciem tuam ad illas.
verses.rendering: If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show them an indulgent face.
translator_notes: The patriarchal anxiety is unmistakable: daughters require physical protection and firm authority. The concern, however controlling by modern standards, reflects the social vulnerability of unmarried women in the ancient world.

verses.text_latin: Trade filiam et grande opus feceris et homini sensato da illam.
verses.rendering: Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have accomplished a great task; give her to a sensible man.
translator_notes: The language of 'giving' a daughter reflects the marriage customs of the period; the emphasis on a 'sensible' (sensatus) husband shifts the priority from wealth to character.

verses.text_latin: Mulier si est tibi secundum animam tuam non proicias illam et odibili non credas te.
verses.rendering: If you have a wife after your own heart, do not cast her out; but do not entrust yourself to one who is hateful.

verses.text_latin: In toto corde tuo honora patrem tuum et gemitus matris tuae ne obliviscaris.
verses.rendering: With all your heart honor your father, and do not forget the groans of your mother.
translator_notes: The 'groans' of the mother refer to the pain of childbirth and the labors of raising children; filial gratitude should be proportional to parental sacrifice.

verses.text_latin: Memento quoniam nisi per illos natus non fuisses et retribue illis quomodo et illi tibi.
verses.rendering: Remember that without them you would not have been born; and repay them as they have given to you.

verses.text_latin: In tota anima tua time Deum et sacerdotes illius sanctifica.
verses.rendering: With all your soul fear God, and honor his priests as holy.
translator_notes: The transition to the priestly section; fear of God naturally extends to reverence for those who serve in his sanctuary.

key_terms.note: Sanctificare here means to treat as sacred, to accord the holiness proper to their office.

verses.text_latin: In tota virtute tua dilige eum qui te fecit et ministros eius ne derelinquas.
verses.rendering: With all your strength love the one who made you, and do not forsake his ministers.
translator_notes: The Shema's three-part formula (heart, soul, strength) is distributed across vv. 29-32, applied to parents, God, and priests.

verses.text_latin: Honora Deum ex tota anima tua et honorifica sacerdotes et propurga te cum brachiis.
verses.rendering: Honor God with all your soul, and show honor to the priests, and purify yourself with the offering of your arms.
translator_notes: 'Arms' (brachia) here refers to the shoulder portions prescribed as priestly offerings in Levitical law.

key_terms.note: Refers to the shoulder/arm portions of sacrificial animals assigned to the priests (cf. Deuteronomy 18:3).

verses.text_latin: Da illis partem sicut mandatum est tibi primitiarum et purgationis et de neglegentia tua purga te cum paucis.
verses.rendering: Give them their portion as commanded to you: the firstfruits and the purification offering; and for your negligence purify yourself with a small offering.
translator_notes: The specific liturgical obligations -- firstfruits and purification -- locate Ben Sira firmly within a functioning temple economy.

key_terms.note: The first and best portion of the harvest, owed to God and distributed to the priests.

verses.text_latin: Datum brachiorum tuorum et sacrificium sanctificationis offeres Domino et initia sanctorum.
verses.rendering: The gift of your arms and the sacrifice of sanctification you will offer to the Lord, together with the holy firstfruits.

verses.text_latin: Et pauperi porrige manum tuam ut perficiatur propitiatio et benedictio tua.
verses.rendering: And stretch out your hand to the poor, so that your atonement and your blessing may be complete.
translator_notes: Charity to the poor completes the liturgical cycle: offerings to God through the priests must be accompanied by care for the destitute.

verses.text_latin: Gratia dati in conspectu omnis viventis et mortuo non prohibeas gratiam.
verses.rendering: The grace of a gift is in the sight of every living person, and from the dead do not withhold kindness.
translator_notes: Care for the dead (proper burial, mourning rites) is a sacred duty; cf. Tobit's insistence on burying the dead at great personal risk.

verses.text_latin: Non desis plorantibus in consolatione et cum lugentibus ambula.
verses.rendering: Do not fail to comfort those who weep, and walk with those who mourn.
translator_notes: Ministry of presence: walking with mourners rather than merely speaking to them.

verses.text_latin: Non te pigeat visitare infirmum ex his enim in dilectione firmaberis.
verses.rendering: Do not be reluctant to visit the sick, for by such deeds you will be strengthened in love.
translator_notes: Visiting the sick strengthens the visitor's capacity for love -- a reciprocal benefit. This became one of the seven corporal works of mercy in Catholic tradition.

verses.text_latin: In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua et in aeternum non peccabis.
verses.rendering: In all your works, remember your last end, and you will never sin.
translator_notes: One of the most quoted verses in Christian ascetical literature. 'Memorare novissima' (remember the last things) became the foundation of the medieval meditation on death. The claim is bold: constant awareness of mortality is the ultimate safeguard against sin.

key_terms.note: The novissima (last things) encompass death, judgment, and whatever lies beyond; the term later gave its name to eschatology (de novissimis).
